body:
A period of major social change

From about the 6th century BCE, northern India experienced important political, economic and intellectual changes. Large territorial states called mahajanapadas developed, towns expanded, trade became more organised, and new religious teachers questioned established beliefs and practices. Jainism and Buddhism grew within this changing society.

A janapada was a territory associated with the settlement of a people or clan. A mahajanapada was a larger and more powerful territorial state. Early Buddhist and Jain texts refer to 16 mahajanapadas, although their lists are not identical.

Many mahajanapadas were monarchies ruled by kings. Others, such as Vajji, followed the gana-sangha form of government, in which several ruling men shared political authority. This was an oligarchic arrangement rather than a democracy with equal voting rights for all adults.

Why towns and new occupations mattered

Agriculture supported the expanding population. In parts of the Ganga valley, iron ploughshares helped cultivate heavy soils, while the transplantation of paddy improved production where water was available. Greater agricultural output could support people who were not themselves cultivators.

Towns consequently brought together different occupational groups, including merchants, artisans, labourers, officials, landholders and religious teachers. Markets and routes connecting settlements enabled goods and ideas to move between regions. The growth of towns is often described as part of the second urbanisation of ancient India, following the much earlier Harappan urban civilisation.

These changes did not automatically produce Jainism and Buddhism. Rather, they created a social environment in which travelling teachers could meet diverse audiences and receive support from householders, merchants and rulers.

Religious questioning and the Shramana tradition

Vedic religious practices included sacrifices conducted by priests. Some elaborate sacrifices required considerable resources and were associated with royal power. Brahmanical texts also prescribed social duties according to varna, a fourfold classification of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras.

Not everyone accepted the authority of priests or the idea that birth should determine religious status. Different thinkers asked whether rituals were sufficient for liberation and whether a person's conduct mattered more than inherited position.

Jainism and Buddhism developed within the wider Shramana tradition, which emphasised personal discipline, renunciation, ethical conduct and liberation from worldly suffering or rebirth. Their teachers questioned the exclusive authority of the Vedas and offered paths that did not depend on performing elaborate Vedic sacrifices.

The emergence of Jainism and Buddhism was connected with urbanisation and dissatisfaction with some established practices, but neither religion was simply an economic protest. Both also addressed fundamental questions about suffering, action, rebirth and liberation.

The significance of this background

The importance of this period lies in the interaction of several developments. States needed resources and administration; towns supported specialised occupations; merchants and householders became important social groups; and religious teachers gained audiences beyond hereditary priestly circles. The resulting religious communities would later influence literature, education, architecture and social values across India.

Prelims focus

  • The major period of change associated with the mahajanapadas was the 6th century BCE.
  • Early Buddhist and Jain texts mention 16 mahajanapadas.
  • Vajji was an important gana-sangha; Magadha became a powerful monarchy.
  • Iron agriculture, expanding towns and trade formed part of the wider historical setting.
  • Jainism and Buddhism belonged to the broader Shramana tradition.
  • Trap: A political gana-sangha was not equivalent to modern universal democracy.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 6, 'Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic', printed pp. 57–62, and Chapter 7, 'New Questions and Ideas', pp. 65–66; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', printed pp. 28–32, and Theme 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings', pp. 84–86.]

title: The Sixth-Century BCE Setting: New States, Towns and Religious Ideas

body:
Conduct became central to religious life

A major social contribution of Jainism and Buddhism was their emphasis on ethical behaviour and personal effort. Both traditions taught that a person's actions have consequences and that spiritual progress requires more than birth, inherited status or the performance of costly rituals.

The traditions did not teach identical methods. Jainism placed exceptionally strict emphasis on non-injury and ascetic discipline, whereas Buddhism taught a path of moderation that rejected both extreme self-indulgence and extreme bodily hardship.

Jain ethics: non-injury and self-restraint

Vardhamana Mahavira, regarded in Jain tradition as the 24th Tirthankara, taught a disciplined path towards liberation. A Tirthankara is a spiritual teacher who shows the way across the cycle of worldly existence.

The central Jain ethical principle is ahimsa, or non-injury to living beings. Jain thought gives careful attention to the lives of humans, animals, plants and even very small forms of life. Consequently, avoiding harm extends beyond the rejection of warfare or deliberate violence to everyday behaviour and occupations.

Jain monks and nuns undertake 5 great vows:

  • Ahimsa: non-violence or non-injury.
  • Satya: truthfulness.
  • Asteya: not stealing.
  • Brahmacharya: celibacy.
  • Aparigraha: non-possession and freedom from attachment to property.

These are strict monastic vows. Jain householders follow corresponding ethical restraints in forms suited to family and occupational life. The distinction is important because not every lay follower is required to live exactly like a monk or nun.

Jainism also explains the path to liberation through right faith, right knowledge and right conduct, collectively called the Three Jewels or Ratnatraya.

Buddhist ethics: moderation and compassion

Gautama Buddha taught that suffering is a fundamental feature of ordinary existence and that craving or attachment contributes to it. This craving is called tanha. Buddhist teaching holds that suffering can cease through the removal of craving and the cultivation of a disciplined way of life.

The Middle Path avoids the extremes of sensual indulgence and severe self-mortification. The Noble Eightfold Path includes right understanding, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. Its ethical components encourage truthful speech, restraint from harmful action and responsible conduct towards others.

The Buddha also emphasised metta, or loving-kindness, and karuna, or compassion. These ideals applied to ordinary relationships. Buddhist teaching encouraged householders and rulers to treat other people humanely, including those working under their authority.

Two related Buddhist ideas are anicca, the impermanence of conditioned things, and anatta, the absence of an eternal, unchanging self. These ideas distinguish Buddhist thought from philosophies that teach an eternal individual soul.

What changed, and what did not

By stressing moral action and spiritual effort, Jainism and Buddhism questioned the belief that ritual privilege or high birth alone established spiritual worth. Their teachings offered religious participation and a sense of moral responsibility to groups beyond hereditary priestly elites.

Nevertheless, religious criticism of birth-based superiority did not eliminate caste distinctions from society. Social hierarchies continued, and the opportunities available to individuals still depended partly on gender, property, family and local customs.

Two meanings of the Three Jewels

In Jainism, the Three Jewels are right faith, right knowledge and right conduct. In Buddhism, the Three Jewels or Three Refuges are the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha. The names are similar, but their components are different.

Prelims focus

  • Mahavira was the 24th Jain Tirthankara.
  • The 5 great Jain monastic vows include ahimsa and aparigraha.
  • Ratnatraya in Jainism means right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.
  • Tanha means craving; the Buddhist Middle Path rejects 2 extremes.
  • Metta means loving-kindness and karuna means compassion.
  • Trap: The Buddhist Three Jewels are Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, not the Jain Ratnatraya.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 7, 'New Questions and Ideas', printed pp. 65–70; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings', sections 'The Message of Mahavira' and 'The Teachings of the Buddha', printed pp. 88–92.]

title: Ethical Teachings and Their Influence on Social Conduct

body:
New religious communities in an expanding urban economy

The growth of trade and towns made merchants, wealthy householders and specialised artisans increasingly visible in public life. Jain and Buddhist communities attracted support from some of these groups. Their support helped teachers travel, sustain monastic communities and eventually establish permanent religious buildings.

The religions did not create agriculture, commerce or towns. These activities already existed and expanded for several reasons. The important relationship is that urban wealth helped support religious institutions, while those institutions became places of teaching, social contact and artistic patronage.

Householders, merchants and guilds

Early Indian texts refer to gahapatis, or substantial householders, often associated with control over household resources and agricultural property. Wealthy merchants also became important donors.

Many merchants and craftspeople organised themselves into associations called shrenis, commonly described as guilds. Their functions included:

  • Providing training and organising work among craftspeople.
  • Obtaining raw materials and distributing finished goods.
  • Coordinating commercial activities among merchants.
  • Accepting deposits and employing funds in ways that could generate income.
  • Supporting religious institutions through donations or income from invested money.

Their economic and religious functions could therefore be connected. A wealthy person might deposit money with a shreni, while part of the resulting income supported a monastery. This does not mean that every guild operated in the same way or that all guilds were religious organisations.

Why merchants supported Jainism and Buddhism

Both traditions valued generosity, disciplined conduct and restraint. Their teachings could appeal to merchants and householders who were not part of the hereditary priestly establishment.

Jainism received substantial support from trading communities. Its strict principle of non-injury could be particularly difficult to follow in occupations such as farming, where cultivation may unintentionally harm insects and other living beings. This helps explain the historical association between Jainism and some merchant communities. It does not mean that all Jains were traders or that cultivators could not become followers.

Buddhist monasteries also received support from a wide range of donors, including rulers, landholders, merchants, craftspeople and other lay followers. Donations might consist of food, clothing, medicines, land or funds for buildings.

The religious sangha

In Buddhism, the Sangha was the organised community of monks and nuns. Monks were called bhikkhus and nuns bhikkhunis. They generally depended on voluntary offerings rather than ordinary household occupations.

Buddhist texts describe members entering the Sangha from different social backgrounds, including merchants, workers, craftspeople and people of high birth. Within the monastic order, members were expected to leave behind previous claims to social rank. According to Buddhist tradition, women were admitted to the monastic order, and Mahapajapati Gotami became the first bhikkhuni.

Monastic entry and life were nevertheless governed by rules. The Buddhist Vinaya Pitaka records disciplinary regulations, and the historical position of monks and nuns was not identical in every respect.

Two different uses of Sangha

A political gana-sangha, such as Vajji, was an association of ruling men who shared political authority. The Buddhist Sangha was a religious monastic community. The common word does not make their functions or membership rules identical.

From temporary shelters to permanent viharas

Early Buddhist and Jain monks often travelled to teach. During the rainy season, travelling became difficult, so they stayed in one place. Temporary shelters and caves gradually gave way, in many locations, to permanent monasteries.

A vihara was a monastic residence. It provided accommodation and a setting for religious instruction and discussion. Supporters supplied necessities, while monks and nuns taught religious principles to interested followers.

Donation inscriptions at Sanchi in present-day Madhya Pradesh show that patronage was not limited to kings. Women, men, monks, nuns and occupational associations contributed to religious monuments. The guild of ivory workers is specifically associated with the financing of part of a gateway at Sanchi.

Mathura likewise developed as a centre of crafts and religious activity. Its inscriptions record donations associated with different occupational groups, and the town had Buddhist monasteries as well as Jain shrines.

Prelims focus

  • Shrenis were associations of merchants or craftspeople.
  • Guilds could organise production, trade, deposits and religious donations.
  • Bhikkhus were Buddhist monks; bhikkhunis were Buddhist nuns.
  • Vinaya Pitaka contains rules for Buddhist monastic life.
  • The ivory workers' guild contributed to a gateway at Sanchi.
  • Trap: A religious Sangha and a political gana-sangha were different institutions.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 7, 'New Questions and Ideas', printed pp. 69–72, and Chapter 9, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns', pp. 89–94; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, sections 'Followers of the Buddha' and 'Stupas', printed pp. 92–97.]
